analysis.one_liner: Taxes stock, bond, and derivative trades at 0.1%, paid by exchanges and brokers.
analysis.headline: A 0.1% tax on stock, bond, and derivative trades, sponsored by six Democratic senators, died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a 0.1% tax on every purchase of stocks, bonds, and derivatives traded on U.S. exchanges or involving U.S. parties — a levy aimed at high-volume trading. Stock and bond exchanges and brokers would collect the tax, and new stock issues and very short-term debt would be exempt. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in July 2023 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the federal treasury would gain revenue from a tax that falls on each trade, meaning the heaviest burden lands on hedge funds, high-frequency traders, and other large investors who buy and sell constantly. Ordinary investors, who trade rarely, would owe little directly, and the public would benefit from whatever the revenue funded. Companies raising money by issuing new stock would not pay the tax on those issuances [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 0.1% excise tax on each covered purchase of stocks, bonds, and derivatives, so frequent, high-volume traders — who move most of the market's volume — pay the most.

Applies to trades on U.S. exchanges or involving U.S. persons, and treats controlled foreign corporations as U.S. persons whose American shareholders must pay the tax, closing an obvious route for shifting trades offshore.
Requires exchanges and brokers to collect and pay the tax, so individual investors generally would not have to file or calculate anything themselves.
Exempts initial issuances of securities, so companies raising capital by selling new stock would not be taxed on that activity.

analysis.who_pays: Large banks, hedge funds, and high-frequency trading firms would bear most of the cost directly, since they trade the most. Part of the cost would likely pass through to ordinary investors, because mutual funds and retirement funds trade on behalf of savers and could pass the tax on through fund expenses. Exchanges and brokers would take on the administrative job of collecting and remitting the tax [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Big banks, hedge funds, high-frequency traders

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to every covered purchase, including trades made by mutual funds and retirement funds, so ordinary savers would absorb part of the cost through higher fund expenses even though they never place a trade themselves.
The bill carves out initial securities issuances and short-term debt with maturities of 100 days or less, which narrows the tax base and concentrates the burden on the secondary trading market.

A transaction tax can push some trading to venues outside the United States; the bill tries to counter this by taxing any trade involving a U.S. person and directing the Treasury Secretary to write anti-avoidance rules, but enforcement would depend on those rules working as intended.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The 0.1% rate is small enough per trade that long-term, buy-and-hold investors would feel little of it, while the burden concentrates on high-volume professional trading — a reasonable design for taxing financial activity. The honest cost is that retirement funds and mutual funds trade constantly on savers' behalf, so some of the tax would flow back to ordinary investors as higher fund expenses, and its anti-offshoring provisions depend on future Treasury rules holding up.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there, with no hearing or vote, until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Brian Schatz introduced the bill on July 25, 2023, joined by five Democratic colleagues: Van Hollen, Warren, Merkley, Whitehouse, and Fetterman.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever taken — the committee never held a markup or vote, and the full Senate never debated it — and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large financial firms and high-volume traders are better off because the bill died, since no new tax was ever imposed on their trades. The senators who sponsored it gained a record of support without needing to move it through a committee they did not chair.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big traders who avoided a new tax

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the effort

for.name: Sens. Van Hollen, Warren, Merkley, Whitehouse, and Fetterman
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; none of them sat in a position to schedule committee action on it

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress — no markup, no hearing on the bill, no vote

against.name: Financial services and trading industry
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed financial transaction taxes in Congress through lobbying

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, no Republican supported it, and the bill never advanced far enough to produce a recorded floor vote.

industries.industry: Securities traders, hedge funds, and high-frequency trading firms
industries.note: The tax hits every covered purchase, so the firms that trade the most pay the most. Their interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the public's interest in the revenue it would raise.

industries.industry: Mutual funds and retirement fund managers
industries.note: Funds trading on behalf of savers would owe the tax on each purchase and would likely pass some of it to ordinary investors through fund expenses, though the tiny per-trade rate would be a small share of fund costs.
Exchanges and brokers are made the collectors of the tax, adding compliance and remittance work for them; the same mechanism spares individual investors from having to file anything.
